## Operations, streams, and exclusions

- Every HTTP operation method, including streaming operations, is generated as a short delegation
  into the hand-written behavior core (ADR-0008).
- Bound root payload-union identity supplies a stream adapter's optional concrete unknown-arm
  metadata and scopes its carrier documentation; an adapter without such a union emits null.
  A stream payload union that reaches known-impossible tags, directly or through a nested union,
  refuses binding by root union, offending union, and tag name, so fallback cannot bypass
  impossible-tag dispatch. The behavior core learns no generated model name or operation identity
  from this wiring (ADR-0038).
- Every generated operation member, `Enumerate*Async` companions included, documents its operation
  identity and its HTTP method and route template in `<remarks>` as text only; no emitter branches
  on the identity (ADR-0008). A cursor-enumeration companion also links to its page operation and
  includes that operation's effective summary: the curated summary; otherwise the upstream summary
  or description, joined when both exist; otherwise the route fallback. The companion's remarks
  contain the route remark, the page operation's curated remarks, a link to the page operation,
  and the effective summary, in that order; its documentation has no separate curation target.
- An internal-raw family emits its clients sealed and internal — internal operation methods and
  handle factory, no mocking constructor — under raw type names, while the root client keeps the
  public family accessor its hand-written door answers. Only such a family may carry a
  document-declared request header: an optional, non-deep-object, unformatted string, plain or
  null-wrapped. It emits as an optional trailing method parameter and travels the declared-header
  channel into the pipeline. The value stays a caller concern and never enters curation or
  generated code; a header-bearing operation forgoes the cursor-enumeration companion (ADR-0013,
  ADR-0021).
- A query binds the `ListRequest` base by inclusion: it must carry the admitted optional `limit`
  (typed `int` by its row), `order`, and `cursor` parameters in their admitted shapes, and every
  further optional parameter binds beside them as its own request property. A missing spine member,
  or one whose schema is not the admitted shape, keeps the request flat and unpaginated.
- A cursor-list operation emits an additive `Enumerate*Async` companion only when binding proves the
  admitted `ListRequest` query, `ListCursor` response, item collection, and operation signature, and
  the query declares no required parameter — a continuation must be constructible from no request at
  all. Generated response adapters project page items, the opaque next cursor, and the continuation
  request into one hand-written traversal core. Method names, descriptions, and upstream source do
  not independently confer pagination semantics (ADR-0013, ADR-0017).
- A query parameter binds by shape: a required parameter becomes a `required`, non-nullable
  request property and makes the request itself a required method and route argument; an optional
  parameter binds nullable and is omitted from the wire when unset, whether or not its schema
  admits JSON null. A query member's description is the parameter schema's own, then its resolved
  target's, so an optional parameter documents itself the same with or without a null arm. A plain
  string binds as the integer its `queryParameterTypes` row names, where upstream's server decodes
  it as a number and upstream's generated client takes one, or as a
  string under a reason-bearing `stringQueryParameters` row; a plain string with neither row fails
  generation, and a row whose parameter the document now declares as a number, or no longer
  carries, fails it too (ADR-0037). The integer travels as its invariant decimal text and the
  server enforces its range. The spine's own value sets (list order, the parent-session filter)
  and the optional deep-object location selector, plain or null-wrapped, bind their spine types. The exact true/false text
  binds `bool?` for an optional parameter and `bool` for a required one, and the route builder
  writes lowercase `true` or `false`; an unset optional is omitted. Any other string enum becomes
  a generated extensible enum whose spelling the route builder writes as given, refusing a default
  value; a value-or-list of such an enum binds a read-only list of it, written as one key per
  element as upstream's client writes an array, and nothing for an unset or empty list; every other
  query shape refuses by name.
- The SSE engine remains hand-written runtime behavior; generated stream methods bind their route,
  payload, frame, declared failure event, typed cause, and statuses from the pin. Cause models,
  converters, array metadata, and adapter metadata pass through the same emitted registry and
  System.Text.Json source-generation compile proof as payload models (ADR-0008, ADR-0015).
- Exclusion is reserved for transports the HTTP pipeline cannot carry, such as a WebSocket upgrade.
  Every excluded operation is fingerprint-pinned so protocol drift forces review (ADR-0008).
- Unknown response media types fail generation. Supported non-JSON response bodies follow the
  fail-closed content-type-to-payload mapping recorded by ADR-0008. An `application/octet-stream`
  success whose schema is `string` with `format: binary` binds a binary envelope: the buffered
  bytes as `Content` (`ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`) and the server's `Content-Type` as `ContentType`,
  materialized without a charset decode; its error statuses keep their JSON bodies (ADR-0029). A
  required `application/octet-stream` request body with the same schema binds as the caller's
  `Stream`, the last wire parameter after a standalone query record, which it never absorbs.

## Serialization and Native AOT

System.Text.Json source generation is mandatory. The generator emits the single serializer
registry used by product code; reflection fallback is not a product path. `IsAotCompatible` is
enabled on every modern target the packages build (`net10.0` and later), where the platform supports
that contract, as a target-framework range rather than a named target (ADR-0003).

The converted union variants' generated readers preserve the registry's materialization rules.
Their concrete-record metadata remains registered for writes and canonical failure reporting.
Prefix-tagged variants, open-model records, unconverted variants and unconverted nested records
continue to use metadata; generated readers add no reflection fallback or public API.
Each reader dispatches its members through fixed groups of twelve over a state struct, so `Read`
grows by one group call per twelve members and no other method grows with a record's width except the
construction: the object initializer that sets every required member keeps a reader within the
analyzer wall up to 65 members.
A base64 binary member reads a JSON null through its registered converter, as the metadata path does.

# Coding Style — hand-written code

Date: 2026-11-03

Binding authoring style for every hand-written line in this repository — product code,
`tools/`, and tests. Generated output is governed by the generator's emitters (ADR-0003);
mechanical formatting is governed by `.editorconfig`. This document governs what neither
can see: how code is decomposed, composed, and shaped.

## 1. The central rule

**Private methods are for local mechanics and narrative flow. Code that carries
behavior, policy, an algorithm, or a concept that deserves a name is extracted into a
named collaborator class.**

Private methods are right for:

- **Narrative helpers** — keeping a public method readable as a short story.
- **Local invariants** — internal state handling no other class needs.
- **Small technical details** — repeated mechanics with no domain meaning.

Red flags that demand extraction:

1. Private methods calling each other in chains — a workflow engine hiding in a class.
2. A private method containing a business rule, a policy, or a branching algorithm.
3. Five or more parameters — the parameter list is a class asking to exist.
4. Mutating three or more fields — temporal coupling.
5. The urge to unit-test a private method independently — extract it and test the class.
6. Generic, meaningless names on privates: `Process`, `Handle`, `Do`, `Execute`, `Run`.

Extraction targets by what the code *is*: a rule → `*Policy` / `*Validator`; an
algorithm → `*Classifier` / `*Calculator` / `*Normalizer`; a traversal → `*Walker` /
`*Projector`; an assembly job → `*Builder` / `*Composer`. Name the concept, not the
mechanism. A class is a unit of *meaning* with a testable contract — not a namespace
for a pile of static steps.

## 2. Interfaces, sealing, and dependency injection

- **Interfaces exist at seams**: filesystem, process, network, console, clock,
  environment, any external system, and cross-module boundaries — the places a test
  substitutes (NSubstitute) or a composition swaps. A seam's interface lives in the
  owning slice's `Abstractions/` folder, next to what it abstracts.
- **Everything else is a `sealed class`.** Pure logic a test can construct directly
  gets no interface ceremony — no `IThing` for a single implementation nobody
  substitutes. The analyzer wall already enforces sealed-by-default (MA0053).
- **One exception: stateless policy is a `static class`.** A policy that is a pure function over
  the data it is given — no I/O, no collaborator, no mutable state — is a static class with static
  methods, because CA1822 and S2325 make a member that touches no instance state static, and an
  instance the type would never use earns nothing. The generator's binding and emission policies
  are the common case. The moment a policy needs a collaborator, I/O or state, it becomes a sealed
  class that receives its collaborators through its constructor: from the `ServiceCollection` in
  an executable, and by hand-written composition in the SDK, which takes no DI dependency
  (`../architecture/platform-and-packaging.md`).
- **Two homes are static because the language puts them there:** native interop declaration
  holders (the `LibraryImport`/`DllImport` entry points of one platform) and extension-method
  containers. They hold declarations and thin forwarding only; any policy or I/O around a native
  call lives in a sealed class behind a seam. A static class that performs I/O or takes a
  collaborator outside these two homes is a defect to fix, not a pattern to follow.
- **DI-first composition.** Every executable has exactly one composition root: a
  `ServiceCollection` that registers each collaborator behind its seam, handed to the
  CLI framework through its DI registrar. Commands and services receive dependencies
  through constructors — no service locators, no static mutable state, and no behavior on
  static classes beyond the stateless policies above. The executable's static composition-root factory is wiring only: it may
  construct/register concrete adapters but performs no I/O itself. A `playground/` app shows the shape a consumer writes, with the SDK calls in view: a console sample is exempt from this composition rule, and an app keeps its host's DI but need not extract policies for readability's sake. The shape:

  ```csharp
  public static class ToolApp
  {
      public static ServiceCollection CreateServices()
      {
          var services = new ServiceCollection();
          services.AddSingleton<IFileSystem, RealFileSystem>();
          services.AddSingleton<IAnsiConsole>(AnsiConsole.Console);
          services.AddSingleton<ToolLoggingOptions>();
          services.AddLogging(logging => logging.SetMinimumLevel(LogLevel.Trace));
          services.AddSingleton<ILoggerProvider, SpectreConsoleLoggerProvider>();
          services.AddSingleton<ILoggerProvider, FileLoggerProvider>();
          services.AddSingleton<ISpecIngestion, SpecIngestion>();
          services.AddSingleton<ICommandInterceptor, GlobalOptionsInterceptor>();
          return services;
      }

      public static async Task<int> RunAsync(string[] args, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
      {
          using var registrar = new DependencyInjectionRegistrar(CreateServices());
          var app = new CommandApp(registrar);
          app.Configure(config => config.AddCommand<GenerateCommand>("generate"));
          return await app.RunAsync(args, cancellationToken);
      }
  }
  ```

- **CLI composition is full-battery, not skeletal.** The single root owns configuration
  and mutable invocation options where needed, every external seam (`IFileSystem`,
  `IAnsiConsole`, process/network collaborators), Microsoft.Extensions.Logging providers,
  application services, and interceptors. Tool logging uses MEL end to end: structured
  `ILogger<T>` consumption, a Spectre-backed console provider, and an optional
  Testably-backed file provider configured by global log-level/log-file settings. Tests
  start from the same production registration path and replace seams after composition;
  they never reproduce the registration list in a parallel test-only root.
- **Cross-cutting CLI options ride an interceptor** (logging verbosity, global options), never
  copy-pasted per command. The composition root registers one exception handler for refusal output
  and exit mapping; commands do not catch refusals. The file-based entry owns Ctrl+C subscription
  and forwards its cancellation token through the composition root to the CLI framework.
- **Statics never perform outside-world operations.** The composition root may instantiate
  and register adapters; actual filesystem, console, time, environment, process, and network
  work occurs only through injected seams. The TestableIO analyzer enforces the filesystem
  half mechanically.

## 3. Signature hygiene

- **No tuple returns** across class boundaries — a result worth returning is worth a
  named record. Tuples are tolerated only inside a method body.
- **No concrete collection parameters** (`List<T>`, `Dictionary<K,V>`) on non-private
  members — accept `IReadOnlyList<T>` / `IReadOnlyDictionary<K,V>` /
  `IEnumerable<T>` or a domain type. Generated wire models expose shallow `IReadOnly*`
  properties without copying caller-owned collections; collaborators that own mutable private
  state still return a snapshot or a read-only view appropriate to that ownership boundary.
- **A parameter cluster traveling together is a record asking to exist** — the same
  three values on four signatures means the domain grew a concept the code has not
  named yet.
- **Guard public inputs** with BCL throw-helpers; assert internal invariants with
  `Debug.Assert` - the repository's defensive-programming default
  (`quality-gates.md`).
- Immutability by default: records with `required`/`init`; name actual collection ownership
  rather than treating `IReadOnly*` as a deep-immutability guarantee. Generated wire models are
  shallow init-only DTOs (ADR-0004/0014); hand-written domain types choose stronger ownership only
  when a concrete consumer or concurrency boundary requires it.
- **Regular expressions:** a regex whose pattern matches in linear time and whose input is
  repository-pinned or test-local passes `Timeout.Infinite` (`matchTimeoutMilliseconds:`), or
  `Regex.InfiniteMatchTimeout` where the API takes a `TimeSpan`. A regex over untrusted input, or
  one whose pattern can backtrack superlinearly, keeps a finite timeout with its reason beside it.
  The match timeout is wall-clock: on a linear pattern over pinned input it guards nothing and fails
  on a stalled runner (#426).

## 4. Layout

- **Vertical feature slices as folders**: a feature's types live together under its
  folder (`Generator/Ingestion/`, `Generator/Binding/`, …), never in horizontal
  type-kind buckets spanning the project.
- **Within a slice, conventional groups**: `Models/` (or the slice's domain-record
  folder) for data shapes, `Abstractions/` for its seams, `Internal/` for the slice's
  implementation where the slice also has a public surface. Similar things sit together; a
  reader predicts where a type lives before opening the tree.
- **The shipped SDK slices by feature with flat namespaces.** Each client family is a
  folder at the project root holding its client, its operation records, its models under
  `Models/` and its implementation under `Internal/`; `Common/` holds the cross-family
  public vocabulary, a root `Internal/` the machinery several slices share, and `Hosting/`
  the server launcher and the background-service doors. Namespaces are API surface and
  folders are placement: a public type declares `OpenCode.Sdk` or `OpenCode.Sdk.Models`
  wherever its file lives, and a file under any `Internal/` folder is internal and declares
  `OpenCode.Sdk.Internal`, with no sub-namespaces. A fail-closed namespace-policy test
  enforces both directions for the SDK project, where IDE0130 is off, so moving a file
  never changes a namespace (ADR-0033).
- The SDK project's root `Internal/` contains area folders only; machinery used by one slice
  lives in that slice's `Internal/` folder.
- `Hosting/Internal/Platform/` is the hosting OS layer: files are placed with their OS siblings
  by OS cohesion, not by consumer count, including the OS helpers used only by the launcher.
- **A test project mirrors the layout of the project under test**: the folder path of a
  SUT predicts the folder path of its tests (`testing-style.md` owns the rule).
- File = type (MA0048) is mechanical everywhere; folder = namespace (IDE0130) is
  mechanical in every project except the SDK, whose namespace-policy test replaces it, and
  `OpenCodeServiceCollectionExtensions.cs` in Extensions, whose DI extension methods declare
  `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` so consumers get `AddOpenCode` without an extra using.
  This document adds the *placement* discipline analyzers cannot see.
- **Split before it hurts:** a class approaching a few hundred lines, or a folder
  flattening into dozens of siblings, is a slice asking to be verticalized. Growth is
  handled by extraction and sub-foldering at the moment of pressure, not by a rewrite
  after the pain.

## 5. Simplicity, calibrated

Take from minimalist ecosystems the product discipline — small surface, few concepts,
no speculative abstraction. Do not take their function-soup idiom into C#: this
repository writes classicist .NET — classes and interfaces, DI, detailed tests against
seams. Both failure modes are named so neither wins:

- **Private-method soup**: one giant class, dozens of private/static steps, `List`
  parameters and tuple returns threading state through a hidden workflow — untestable
  except end-to-end. A known LLM-generation failure mode; review rejects it on sight.
- **Enterprise cosplay**: interfaces, factories, and layers wrapped around code with
  one caller and one shape. Extraction needs a *reason* from §1's red flags; a seam
  needs a *substitution* someone actually performs.

## 6. Enforcement

The analyzer wall already carries part of this document: MA0051 (method length), CA1501, CA1502
and CA1505 (inheritance depth, cyclomatic complexity, maintainability),
MA0048/IDE0130 (file/folder discipline), MA0053 (sealed), CA1062 (guards), the TestableIO analyzer
(I/O seam). No rule measures class length; review enforces what this document
states and the wall does not measure — and in agent-driven development, the executing
agent's plan carries these rules as constraints, so violations are defects, not style
preferences.

# Developing on Windows

Date: 2026-11-06

Operational guidance for a Windows workstation. Everything here is about the developer's machine;
the test suite's own isolation rules live in `testing-style.md` and the gates in `quality-gates.md`.
A fresh worktree is prepared as `quality-gates.md` describes before its first gate; a workstation
keeps one Bun, and when that is not the pinned one the gate runs with the Bun mismatch switch that
`quality-gates.md` describes.

A server started by hand, for example to check HQ, inherits the shell's environment, and isolated
XDG roots don't change that: a provider variable such as `AWS_PROFILE` makes a cold server pick
that provider's model as its default, and the first turn then fails on missing credentials. Clear
such variables before starting it; the suite's own live runs already do (`testing-style.md`).

## Native AOT publishing

The gate's `NativeAot` pass publishes a consumer with ILCompiler, which links with the platform
linker: a workstation needs the Visual Studio Build Tools workload "Desktop development with C++"
(MSVC and a Windows SDK). Without it the publish fails with "Platform linker not found".

With the Visual Studio 2026 Build Tools, ILCompiler finds the linker through `VsDevCmd.bat`, which
calls `vswhere.exe` by its bare name from the Visual Studio Installer folder. The packed-consumer
fixture puts that folder on its publish's `PATH` itself. A native AOT publish run by hand, from a
shell that sets `NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath` and has no Installer folder on `PATH`, fails
with "'vswhere.exe' is not recognized" inside the linker command and then MSB3073: put
`C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\Installer` on that process's `PATH` rather than
clearing the variable.

## Live legs against a Linux-hosted server

The `opencode-pty` daemon (`@opencode/pty`) ships a win32 package too, so a persistent PTY live
run directly on Windows drives the round trip. To prove the live leg against a Linux server from a
Windows workstation, `PinnedOpenCodeServerFixture`'s external-endpoint mode plus
`PersistentPtyDaemonGate`'s override run it against a server hosted in WSL2.

Clone into the WSL filesystem instead of reusing the Windows checkout over `/mnt/<drive>`: one
shared `external/opencode/node_modules` holds the platform package of whichever OS installed last,
so the two installs clobber each other's daemon binary.

1. In WSL2, clone the repository and initialize the submodule:
   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/opencode-dotnet/opencode-sdk-dotnet.git ~/repos/opencode-sdk-dotnet
   cd ~/repos/opencode-sdk-dotnet
   git submodule update --init --depth 1 external/opencode
   ```
2. Install the bun the pin names in its `packageManager` field, not the workstation's own:
   ```sh
   curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash -s "bun-v$(grep -o '"packageManager": *"bun@[0-9.]*"' \
     external/opencode/package.json | grep -o '[0-9][0-9.]*')"
   ```
3. Install the dependencies — this is what places `@opencode/pty-<platform>/bin/opencode-pty`,
   which `packages/core` resolves as its `binaryPath`:
   ```sh
   cd ~/repos/opencode-sdk-dotnet/external/opencode
   bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts
   ```
4. Serve from `packages/cli` under isolated XDG roots and a fixed password, so the run touches no
   real profile and the Windows side can authenticate:
   ```sh
   cd ~/repos/opencode-sdk-dotnet/external/opencode/packages/cli
   mkdir -p /tmp/ocsdk/data /tmp/ocsdk/cache /tmp/ocsdk/config /tmp/ocsdk/state
   XDG_DATA_HOME=/tmp/ocsdk/data XDG_CACHE_HOME=/tmp/ocsdk/cache \
   XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/tmp/ocsdk/config XDG_STATE_HOME=/tmp/ocsdk/state \
   OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT='{}' OPENCODE_DISABLE_MODELS_FETCH=1 OPENCODE_PASSWORD=<pw> \
     bun src/index.ts serve --port 4097
   ```
5. On Windows, point the fixture at it and run the persistent PTY legs:
   ```powershell
   $env:OPENCODE_SDK_TESTS_ENDPOINT = "http://localhost:4097"
   $env:OPENCODE_SDK_TESTS_PASSWORD = "<pw>"
   $env:OPENCODE_SDK_TESTS_PTY_DAEMON = "1"
   dotnet test --project "$PWD/tests/OpenCode.Sdk.Tests/OpenCode.Sdk.Tests.csproj" --configuration Release --no-build `
     -- --treenode-filter "/*/*/PersistentPtyLiveTests/*" --report-trx
   ```

The filter keeps the run to the live legs, which is what the recipe was proven with; the whole suite
can also run against the same endpoint, because the fixture-driven live legs create their sessions
without a Windows location, so no path from the workstation reaches the WSL2 server. The
blank-password guard is real: an unset or whitespace `OPENCODE_SDK_TESTS_PASSWORD` fails
initialization by name rather than reaching the server.

The exact-pin discipline is the operator's: the WSL2 server must be built from the same submodule
commit; the fixture prints both so a mismatch is visible, it cannot verify a source run's version.

## Driving WSL from a Windows shell

Put the WSL side in a script file and run it as `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 wsl.exe -- bash
/mnt/c/<path>.sh` — Git Bash otherwise mangles the quoting and rewrites `/tmp` paths into Windows
ones. Stop the server by pattern (`pkill -f "index.ts serve --port 4097"`) rather than by a pid
file, because a backgrounded `setsid nohup … &` leaves the file empty; the `opencode-pty` daemon
exits with the server.

# Deviation Protocol

Date: 2026-11-02

> *"No plan survives first contact with the enemy."* — Helmuth von Moltke

What to do when implementation reality contradicts current canon, an approved plan, or a sealed
decision.
This is the process rendering of the repo's engineering default — fail loudly rather than
guess; silent fallbacks only as explicitly recorded tolerances in current canon. An executing
agent never silently codes around a contradiction, and never silently "fixes" a sealed
design back toward convention.

## The ladder

Classify the deviation before acting. When in doubt between two levels, take the higher.

### Level 0 — Implementation detail

Current canon and the approved plan are silent, or the question sits below their resolution (a
private helper's name, test internals, a local refactor). **Decide and move on.** Note it in the
PR description only if a reviewer might wonder.

A departure from upstream's first-party behaviour at the pin is never level 0, even where canon is
silent: whether to diverge is the maintainer's decision (`../architecture/client-runtime.md`, ADR-0031). Bring it
as level 2 with the evidence, the options, and a recommendation, and wait.

### Level 1 — Recorded fallback

The chosen mechanism fails, but current architecture or an ADR records a fallback or reversal
trigger for exactly this case.
**Execute the recorded fallback.** Pre-authorized — no stop needed, but the slice PR must
state that the trigger fired, and the documents the fallback touches are corrected in the
same change. Add a research-log entry when the evidence is worth keeping.

### Level 2 — Canonical correction

Reality contradicts a current non-decision claim — operational state, `GLOSSARY.md`, an active
plan's binding constraint, or a verified research fact — and no fallback is recorded:
upstream behaves differently, an API does not exist, a count is wrong, a detail cannot be
built as written. **Stop the affected task** (neighboring tasks may continue if
untouched). Capture the evidence — commands, output, source references. Propose the
correction to the maintainer; on approval, the document is corrected in place and the
task resumes. Evidence worth keeping goes to the research log; a correction that does not land in
this change gets a record under the findings rule in `workflow.md`.

Vision and reference documents in the private companion repository (design explorations and
specs that no approved plan binds) are not protocol subjects: contradicting one is a level-0 note
in the PR, and the document is corrected opportunistically. A binding constraint of the plan the
maintainer approved for the current work (a named mechanism, order, or scope) is not reference
material: contradicting it is level 2, and the mechanism is never swapped without the maintainer.

### Level 3 — Locked-decision challenge

New evidence contradicts a normative architecture or engineering decision, or an ADR.
**Stop the slice.**
Bring the evidence to the maintainer; the decision is re-litigated in a research/grill
pass — from mechanisms and sources, per the working agreements. The outcome is either a
superseding/amended ADR or a recorded confirmation. Locked decisions are reopened by
evidence, never by convenience.

## Rules that apply at every level

- **Escalation path:** a subagent reports the contradiction to its orchestrating session;
  the session classifies the level and, at level 2+, stops and involves the maintainer.
  Subagents never self-resolve level 2+.
- **A deviation without a trace is a defect**, even when the deviation itself was right.
- **The docs pass is part of the deviation, not follow-up work:** whichever document
  carried the contradicted claim is corrected in the same change
  (`documentation.md`).

# Documentation

Date: 2026-11-09

Canonical rules for documentation ownership, authority, lifecycle, references, and lossless
maintenance.

## Document roles

| Role | Homes | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Agent entry point | `AGENTS.md` | Universal operating rules and task-to-canon routing only |
| Current architecture | `docs/architecture/` | Normative current technical decisions |
| Current engineering practice | `docs/engineering/` | Normative current authoring, quality, workflow, and documentation rules |
| Decision rationale | `docs/adr/` | Accepted decision context, trade-offs, consequences, and reversal triggers |
| Domain vocabulary | `GLOSSARY.md` | Current terms and explicitly avoided synonyms |
| Operational state | `docs/ROADMAP.md` | What is done, next, open, and known to be incomplete; shrinks as work lands |
| Protocol provenance | `spec/SNAPSHOT.md` | Exact upstream pin and refresh procedure |
| Consumer documentation | `README.md`, `docs/guide/`, `CHANGELOG.md` | How to use the shipped packages, complete on its own (Consumer documentation, below) |

Dated research evidence and session operations live in a private companion repository
(`opencode-dotnet/opencode-sdk-dotnet-internal`); the canonical documentation here is complete
without it.

Repository files and current canonical documents beat memory, dated research, transient plans, and
handoffs. If two current canonical sources appear to disagree, do not pick a winner silently; use
the deviation protocol.

## One canonical home

Every current fact has one canonical owner. Other appearances are short relays that link to the
owner instead of restating the full rule. Change-prone values are read from their mechanical source
instead of copied into prose.

Documentation refactors are lossless relocations, not summarization exercises. Preserve useful,
unique information in an appropriate canonical, rationale, evidence, or operational home. Delete a
passage only after proving it is an exact duplicate, obsolete without historical value, or retained
in a more authoritative source. Git history is not a substitute for accessible, useful canon.

Current-state documents describe the status quo rather than narrating their amendment history.
Dated research preserves the history and may state decisions later superseded; it must never be
used as current policy without following its links to current canon. ADRs record decision rationale,
not work-queue state.

## Dates and lifecycle

Every hand-written document under `docs/` carries a `Date:` line.

- In current-state and operational documents, `Date:` is the latest substantive update.
- In ADRs, `Date:` is the date of the decision represented by the current record; a material
  decision revision moves it, while an editorial link correction does not.
- Where a `Date:` records a historical snapshot rather than a current state, an editorial
  correction does not rewrite it.

A sentence that must change when a task completes belongs in `docs/ROADMAP.md` or a temporary
handoff, not in evergreen architecture or engineering canon. Keep affected documentation current in
the same change as code; documentation is not follow-up work.

## References

References point one way: documentation may cite code, but code artifacts never cite documentation.
Comments in source, project files, `.editorconfig`, workflows, and generated files explain the
status quo locally; they do not point to movable prose or narrate decision history.
Curation rows cite a canon section with a proven excerpt; other artifacts that cite documentation are open debt (#202).

Canonical documents — architecture, engineering, ADRs, and `GLOSSARY.md` — never point at the
private companion repository's paths or numbering (research-log questions, sessions, document
numbers) or at `docs/ROADMAP.md` content, which moves as work lands. Dated evidence is cited inline
by date and title, for example: internal research, 2026-08-24, "Runtime pipeline architecture
design". Naming the ROADMAP as the home of operational state, as the table above and `AGENTS.md`
do, is routing, not a reference.

Audience decides placement. Knowledge for consumers of the packages belongs in the consumer
documentation; knowledge shared by maintainers and agents belongs in architecture, engineering,
ADR, domain, or operational documents; guidance needed only by coding agents belongs in
`AGENTS.md` or the private companion repository.

ADRs are created lazily under the criteria in `docs/adr/README.md`. Handovers are consumed against
live Git and GitHub, then deleted when the follow-up ships or a newer handoff supersedes them.

## Consumer documentation

`README.md`, `docs/guide/` and `CHANGELOG.md` speak to people using the packages.

- A change that alters what a consumer sees updates the guide or README section that describes it,
  in the same pull request.
- Every `csharp` fence in `README.md` and `docs/guide/` compiles in CI (`SnippetCompileGuard`), except
  a deliberate fragment, which carries `<!-- snippet: fragment -->` on the line directly above its
  fence; use it only where no complete form exists.
- `CHANGELOG.md` gets an entry under `[Unreleased]` for every user-facing change, in the same pull
  request. A released section is the delta from the previous published package: it states the
  status quo a consumer upgrading from that package meets, never the order of intermediate commits
  or nightlies. A release that moves the protocol pin lists what changed in the protocol under
  `### 🔌 Protocol changes`, and marks each generated-type break **breaking** there, not again under
  `### 💥 Breaking changes`, which holds the hand-written breaks (ADR-0034).
- Consumer documentation names upstream where the server's behaviour matters, but never sends a
  reader to upstream's code, issues or documentation to learn how the SDK behaves; what a consumer
  needs is stated here.

# Slop Review

Date: 2026-11-02

What slop means in this repository, how to recognize it, and the rubric that every change and
every review applies. It complements `coding-style.md` and `testing-style.md`: they say how to
write code and tests, and this file says how to recognize text that should not have been written.
The evidence and the tooling assessment behind it are in internal research, 2026-10-15, "AI slop in
opencode-sdk-dotnet: definition, evidence, catalog, tooling, rubric".

## Definition

**Slop** is code, a test, configuration or prose whose cost to verify and maintain exceeds the
value it adds. It compiles, passes the gate and looks plausible, yet it has at least one of these
properties:

- **removable:** deleting or simplifying it loses no behaviour and no information;
- **unrequested:** no stated purpose of the change needs it;
- **out of place:** it ignores an existing API, seam, convention or canon rule;
- **unproven:** no test would fail if it were wrong, or its author cannot explain it.

Every line that reaches `master` needs someone who can vouch for it.

Slop differs from technical debt. Debt is a deliberate, priced trade-off that announces itself
through friction. Slop is usually nobody's decision. It looks clean and green, and it grows with
volume and with parallel work that cannot see its own prior art. It is prevented at the gate and
swept continuously; it is not paid down later.

## Not slop here

These look like slop to a generic pass and are not:

- `ConfigureAwait(false)` in product code: the analyzer policy requires it.
- A one-implementation internal interface that tests substitute. It is a seam (`coding-style.md`
  §2), though R2 below still applies when it duplicates a BCL abstraction.
- Generated output's own shape. It is judged as shipped product, and fixed in the generator or the
  curation, never by hand (`../architecture/protocol-and-generation.md`).
- A faithful port of upstream behaviour that canon records (`../architecture/client-runtime.md`).
- An `#if` that an analyzer rule forces on one target framework.
- A suppression that follows the suppression policy below.

## Catalog

Each pattern has an ID that reviews and findings cite. Severity follows impact: **H** hides wrong
behaviour or makes a gate lie, **M** costs maintainability or consistency across slices, and **L**
is noise.

### Production code

| SLOP-02 | A near-duplicate helper or idiom in another slice | M |
| SLOP-03 | A speculative abstraction: an interface, factory or options type with no named reason | M |
| SLOP-04 | A one-call wrapper that adds no policy, or a half-applied abstraction | L–M |
| SLOP-05 | Misplaced defence: guards on internal invariants, missing guards at real boundaries | L / H |
| SLOP-06 | Error masking: catch and continue, catch and return a default, a comment-only catch | H |
| SLOP-07 | A silent fallback chain that turns a failure into a valid-looking result | H |
| SLOP-08 | A null-forgiving `!` with no stated guarantee | M |
| SLOP-09 | Comment slop: restating, history narration, plan residue, a stale rationale | L / M when stale |
| SLOP-10 | Dead code and leftovers from an abandoned approach | M |
| SLOP-11 | Scope creep: a drive-by rewrite, an unrequested option or feature | M |
| SLOP-12 | `CancellationToken.None` or `default` passed to get past a rule | M |

## Rubric

Apply the rubric per file or per slice, after the gate is green. Do not flag what the gate already
catches. Each item is pass, fail or not applicable, and a fail names its reason.

### Production code

- **R1. It earns its place.** Deleting or simplifying the construct would lose behaviour or
  information. A wrapper exists because it adds policy, such as error mapping that callers rely on.
- **R2. One abstraction per concern.** Look in the BCL, Polyfill and the existing seams first. A
  substituted seam that duplicates `TimeProvider`, for example, fails this item even though it
  passes R3.
- **R3. Every interface names its reason:** a seam that tests substitute, a public extension
  point, or DI composition.
- **R4. Guard at boundaries, trust nullable annotations inside.** Public entry points guard their
  arguments. Internal code does not re-check what the annotations prove.
- **R5. No masked errors.** A catch rethrows, filters, or converts the error into a typed outcome
  the caller sees. It never returns a default. A best-effort swallow follows the suppression policy
  below.
- **R6. No silent fallback.** A degraded path is visible to the caller or in the result.
- **R7. Every `!` states its guarantee** in one sentence, or it goes.
- **R8. Cancellation flows.** `CancellationToken.None` appears only with a stated reason, for
  example a shutdown that must finish after the caller cancelled.
- **R9. Comments say why, in the present tense.** No restating, no plan numbers, no history, no
  documentation paths (`documentation.md`, References). A rationale stays true for the code beside
  it.
- **R10. One source per policy constant,** including values that upstream parity fixes.
- **R11. Scope.** Every hunk traces to the stated purpose of the change.
- **R12. Suppressions follow the policy below.**
- **R13. Background work has an owner and a fault path.** A task that is started and not awaited
  is either stored and observed by its owner, or its comment states what owns it and where its
  faults go, and the code backs that claim.
- **R14. A multi-target fork earns its place.** Each `#if` names the API gap that Polyfill and the
  platform helpers do not cover, or the analyzer rule that forces it.
- **R15. Every process, handle and disposable has a named owner.** No disposable is captured by a
  discarded task.

### Tests

- **T1. The oracle comes from upstream evidence:** the spec, upstream source, or an observed frame
  kept as test data. It is never pasted from our own output.
- **T2. The test fails if the change is reverted.** A fix shows red, then green. Characterization
  tests that pin behaviour a rewrite keeps are proven by a named mutant instead of T2's
  red-then-green.
- **T3. Assertions state intent and print a useful failure.** A collection assertion reports the
  elements it saw; `Assert.That(x.Any(…)).IsTrue()` reports only `false`.
- **T4. Arrange goes through builders.** The second copy of a literal grows a builder verb.
- **T5. Existing assertions are not weakened** in a fix without a recorded decision and the upstream
  evidence that the old expectation was wrong.
- **T6. Assert the contract,** not implementation detail.
- **T7. The event decides, never the clock** (`testing-style.md` §6).
- **T8. The case is reachable** through the public contract or the wire format.
- **T9. String-shaping code has boundary cases:** separators at both ends, and escape characters
  next to quotes.

### Prose and configuration

- **P1.** One canonical home, with relays elsewhere. No duplicated globs or conditions, and one
  shared reason instead of copies.
- **P2.** A `<summary>` says what the member is for, in more than its name, in about 40 words or
  fewer. Mechanism detail goes in `<remarks>`.

## Suppression policy

A suppression silences a gate, so it is rare, visible and counted:

- **It names the rule and its reason,** and the reason is true for the code beside it.
- **It has the maintainer's approval.** A new suppression is called out in the pull request body.
- **One channel per rule per file.** The channels are:
  - `[SlopwatchSuppress]` and `slopwatch-ignore`;
  - `#pragma warning disable`;
  - `[SuppressMessage]`;
  - `.editorconfig` severities, `.globalconfig` and `<NoWarn>`.
- **It is counted.** The suppression ledger test fails on any change the ledger does not show, so
  the ledger moves in the same pull request as the suppression.
- **A best-effort swallow** is a failure the caller cannot act on, such as cleanup after the
  outcome is already decided. It uses a reason-bearing `[SlopwatchSuppress("SW003", "...")]` that
  says where the failure is observed. A discarded `Try…` result is not a substitute.
- **A suppression that no longer suppresses anything is removed,** and so is one whose reason is
  no longer true.

The preferred order is the code fix, then a narrow per-rule arbitration that names the winning rule
(`quality-gates.md`, Analyzer policy), then a suppression.

## How review uses this

- A reviewer judges independently before reading the pull request description, cites catalog IDs
  and rubric items, and flags only what is above a confidence bar.
- A reviewer from a different model family than the author's reviews every change that a model
  drafted.
- Every finding the change does not fix gets a record (`workflow.md`, Findings).

- A pull request joins the queue once the `CI result` check of its own head is green. The queue
  tests it again on top of current `master` and the entries ahead of it, and merges only on that
  green, except when the recorded tested-tree proof and self-vouching guard in `quality-gates.md`
  permit reuse of its green PR result. Otherwise the repository guards count exactly over every
  test file, so a green result from an older base is not enough. After the merge, the work is done
  when the CI the merge commit triggers on
  `master` is green; a merge of only Markdown or `LICENSE` triggers none, and its queue result
  stands.
- CI runs on every pull request and queue entry. A change that touches only Markdown or `LICENSE`
  passes without the build and test jobs. Never put `[skip ci]` in a pull request's commits: the
  required check would not report, and the pull request could not join the queue.

## 🚀 The SDK starts the server

`OpenCodeServer.StartAsync()` launches a private `opencode serve` child, waits for it to report
readiness, mints its credential, and hands you an owner object. No ambient proc

var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddOpenCode(options =>
{
    options.Endpoint = server.Endpoint;
    options.Password = server.Password;
});

using var host = builder.Build();
await host.RunAsync();

The `OpenCodeServer` handle stays yours, and the `await using` around `RunAsync` is what ends it:
the server is disposed after the host has stopped, so no hosted service loses its server while it
shuts down. Disposal ends a started child; a discovered service keeps running.

Do not hand the handle to the container with `AddSingleton(server)` instead. A container disposes
only the instances it created, never one you registered, so a started server would outlive the host
until the launcher's own process-death protection ends it. Registering `server.CreateClient()` as a
singleton on its own registers only the root; calling `AddOpenCode` also registers any missing
families from that root without replacing it. An instance you supply this way remains yours to
dispose.

## OPENCODE001

The `ExperimentalClient` (`client.Experimental`) and the types only it uses: session stats, import

# 🖥️ Terminals

Date: 2026-11-10

opencode has two terminal families, and they are genuinely different animals:

| | **PTY** | **Persistent PTY** |
|---|---|---|
| Owned by | the server process | the `opencode-pty` daemon |
| Keyed by | its own id | a session id |
| Survives a server restart | no | yes, through a handoff |
| Output on the wire | text frames | raw bytes |
| Input | `SubmitAsync(string)`, or raw `WriteAsync(string)` | `SubmitAsync(string)`, or raw `WriteAsync(ReadOnlyMemory<byte>)` |
| Resize | `PtyClient.UpdateAsync` with `Size`, over HTTP | `PersistentPtyClient.UpdateAsync` with `Size`, or `ResizeAsync` on the socket |
| Available on Windows | ✅ yes | ✅ yes, from opencode 2.1.x — [when the daemon is unavailable](#-when-the-daemon-is-unavailable) |

Both live sessions ride a **WebSocket**, not the HTTP pipeline. They are the only two doors in the
SDK that do, and they are hand-written for exactly that reason — a socket upgrade cannot be
generated from an OpenAPI document.
